extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature; readers of annotated/critical editions of early-18th-century periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary for understanding/producing early-18th-century periodical essays (specifically Steele's Tatler): authorial purpose, structure, style, publication logistics, and indicators of reception. Useful for editors, literary historians, and writers modelling such periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose of the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: "The general purpose of this paper, is to expose the false arts of life, to pull off the disguises of cunning, vanity, and affectation, and recommend a general simplicity in our dress, our discourse, and our behaviour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The periodical should aim at moral/social correction by exposing affectation and promoting simplicity across manners, dress, discourse, and behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target readership and civic instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper "should be principally intended for the use of politic persons... whereby such worthy and well-affected members of the commonwealth may be instructed, after their reading, what to think; which shall be the end and purpose of this my paper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should instruct politically minded readers, shaping opinion and offering guidance on public matters rather than merely reporting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment for women
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have also resolved to have something which may be of entertainment to the fair sex"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include material specifically appealing to female readers alongside political instruction to broaden audience reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular publication schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: "publish such my advices and reflections every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday in the week for the convenience of the post."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent, frequent schedule (three times weekly here) to build readership and fit postal rhythms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical structure and datelined sections
rubrics_metrics.description: "All accounts of gallantry, pleasure, and entertainment, shall be under the article of White's Chocolate-house; poetry, under that of Will's Coffee-house; learning, under the title of Grecian; foreign and domestic news... from St. James's Coffee-house; and what else I shall on any other subject offer, shall be dated from my own apartment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize content into predictable topical datelines (coffee‑house bylines) so readers know where to look for particular subjects; use a consistent internal taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing and distribution policy
rubrics_metrics.description: "to take it in for the present gratis, and hereafter at the price of one penny, forbidding all hawkers to take more for it at their peril."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with free distribution to gain audience, then set an accessible price; control hawker pricing. Consider production costs when setting price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wide correspondence and contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele states he "had settled a correspondence in all parts of the known and knowing world" and acknowledges "very many incidents which were written by unknown correspondents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit and incorporate letters/correspondence from diverse sources and anonymous contributors to enrich content and create the impression of wide intelligence-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of major assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: He acknowledges particular assistance (e.g., Dr. Swift, a nameless gentleman—Addison) and lists contributions such as the "distinguishing characters... Musical Instruments, the Distress of the News-writers..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where significant help exists, acknowledge collaborators in a preface or notes; identify major contributions even if some helpers remain unnamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: treat common subjects in a new way
rubrics_metrics.description: "[Obvious and common subjects], though at the same time obliged to treat of them in a new and unbeaten method."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merely repeating commonplace material — reframe ordinary topics with fresh perspective or inventive treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a fictitious persona to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of the name Isaac Bickerstaff "gained an audience" and the Bickerstaff persona helped secure reputation and readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a consistent authorial persona or pseudonym to create identity, authority, and marketable voice for the periodical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit must serve a useful or honourable end
rubrics_metrics.description: "for wit, if a man had it, unless it be directed to some useful end, is but a wanton frivolous quality... all that one should value himself upon in this kind is, that he had some honourable intention in it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize wit that advances moral, instructive, or socially beneficial aims rather than mere cleverness for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality across party lines
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have with the utmost frankness allowed merit wherever I found it, though joined in interests different from those for which I have declared myself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain fairness in commendation and criticism; avoid letting party allegiance wholly determine judgments of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship to avoid offending superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: "I shall... not speak of anything until it is passed, for fear of divulging matters which may offend our superiors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise prudence about publishing potentially offensive material—delay or omit items that risk provoking powerful figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform-oriented targets (social vices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele declares a mission "in extirpating gamesters and duellists" and laments the precarious condition of the English gentleman vis-à-vis gambling and duelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use essays to campaign against specific social vices and to defend the social order or the honour of certain classes when relevant to the paper's moral aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of success and reader reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of popularity cited: "success... successive numbers were reprinted in Dublin and in Edinburgh... long subscription list prefixed to the reprint... copies printed on 'royal'... authorised cheap edition... pirated edition..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact by reprints, regional reissues, subscription lists, multiple paper sizes/editions, and existence of unauthorized copies as signals of wide readership and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfalls for imitators: copying garnish vs. substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay observed imitators thought "that what was only the garnish of the former Tatlers was that which recommended them, and not those substantial entertainments which they everywhere abound in."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid superficial imitation (style or ornament) without reproducing the substantive moral or intellectual content that made the original successful.
